original_question: In the linear model where an algorithm for a transformation is a product of matrices R_t and each step R_t is block diagonal with n-2 identity blocks and one 2x2 unitary block acting on only two coordinates, let F be the normalized n x n Fourier transform, let G = [[0, F], [-F^*, 0]], and define X_alpha = (cos alpha) Id + (sin alpha) G on C^(2n). What is the true asymptotic lower bound, as alpha tends to 0, on the number of such two-coordinate unitary steps required to compute X_alpha? In particular, can one prove that computing X_alpha requires essentially Omega(n log n) steps rather than only the currently derived Omega(alpha^2 n log n) or Omega(alpha n log n) lower bounds?
target_in_paper: The unnumbered open problem in Section 2.2 (“Stronger improvements?”), read together with the setup in Section 2 and the refined lower bound plus footnote in Section 2.1: for the matrices G and X_alpha, can one prove a lower bound stronger than Omega(alpha n log n), with the author’s footnoted conjectural target being Omega((n log n)/log(1/alpha))?
correct_elements: Your draft correctly identifies the relevant part of the paper: the linear two-coordinate unitary-gate model, the normalized Fourier matrix F, the block skew-Hermitian matrix G = [[0, F], [-F^*, 0]], the unitary family X_alpha = (cos alpha) Id + (sin alpha) G on C^(2n), and the fact that the paper derives first an Omega(alpha^2 n log n) lower bound and then an Omega(alpha n log n) improvement. It also correctly recognizes that the paper is asking for a substantially stronger lower bound for computing X_alpha.
missing_details: When computing X_alpha, the ambient space is C^(2n), so each gate R_t should be a 2n x 2n unitary acting nontrivially on only two coordinates; equivalently, it is the identity on the other 2n-2 coordinates. Saying 'n-2 identity blocks' is dimensionally inconsistent for this part of the paper.
The field is C, F is the normalized n x n discrete Fourier transform, and alpha is a real angle.

The paper’s nearest official open question is not 'prove essentially Omega(n log n)'; the explicit question in Section 2.2 is whether one can beat the Omega(alpha n log n) bound, while footnote 1 makes the conjectured sharp target more precise as Omega((n log n)/log(1/alpha)).
The asymptotic lower bound in the paper is a joint statement in n and alpha, not only an alpha -> 0 statement with n suppressed.
The group-law identity X_alpha' X_alpha = X_(alpha+alpha') is part of the nearby context, because it motivates the failed 'squaring trick' heuristic behind the conjectured log-loss bound.

The paper’s model is about computing the action of X_alpha on vectors via a product X_alpha = R_m ... R_1 in the same coordinate space, not about symbolic matrix powering or unrestricted circuit constructions.

The informal sentence in Section 2 that X_alpha should require 'not much smaller than Omega(n log n)' is sharpened by footnote 1; the refined stand-alone question should use the footnoted bound rather than the vaguer informal wording.
refined_question: Let F be the normalized n x n discrete Fourier transform over C, define G = [[0, F], [-F^*, 0]] in C^(2n x 2n), and for real 0 < alpha < pi/4 let X_alpha = (cos alpha) I_(2n) + (sin alpha) G. In the linear model where computing X_alpha means factoring X_alpha = R_m ... R_1 with each R_t in U(2n) acting nontrivially on only two coordinates (equivalently, identity on the other 2n-2 coordinates), is it true that every such computation requires m = Omega((n log n)/log(1/alpha)) steps as alpha -> 0?
justification: This 4-page arXiv note does not contain numbered statements such as Conjecture 1.1, Proposition 1.2, or Theorem 1.3; the relevant target is instead the unnumbered question at the end of Section 2.2. Section 2 defines G and X_alpha and derives the basic Omega(alpha^2 n log n) lower bound. Section 2.1 improves this to Omega(alpha n log n) and, in footnote 1, states the author’s more precise conjecture that the correct bound is Omega((n log n)/log(1/alpha)). Section 2.2 then explicitly asks whether one can obtain a stronger lower bound than Omega(alpha n log n), motivated by a 'squaring trick' heuristic that would suggest the same log-loss bound if it were applicable. Because of that footnote and heuristic, the paper-faithful sharpening of your draft is not an unconditional 'essentially Omega(n log n)' formulation, but the more precise conjectural Omega((n log n)/log(1/alpha)) lower bound for small alpha.
